title: ‘Industry,’ ‘Doctor Who’ Producer Jane Tranter on Resisting Trends, Centering Women and Telling Stories About ‘People Being Accepted for Who They Choose to Be’
description: “Industry” and “Doctor Who” producer Jane Tranter has made a career of going against the grain, and at Rome’s MIA Market on Tuesday, she told Europ
body:
“Industry” and “Doctor Who” producer Jane Tranter has made a career of going against the grain, and at Rome’s MIA Market on Tuesday, she told European producers that the only way to survive in uncertain times is to “go in the opposite direction of everyone else’s traffic.”

	“If everyone else is zigging, you zag. Because at some point, they’re going to want your zag because they’ve run out of zigs,” she said. “We have to be ready for it.”
	

	Appearing in conversation with MIA’s head of drama content Paolo Ciccarelli, Tranter dished on her career as a ground-breaking TV producer, rising through the ranks of British television to become head of drama at the BBC before going on to launch her award-winning production company Bad Wolf with co-founder Julie Gardner in 2015. 


	Opening up about her early days in the industry in the 1990s, Tranter recalled her time as a drama script editor at ITV franchise Carlton Television, when she was told that “no drama that had a female protagonist was ever going to draw an audience.” Before long, however, she joined a cohort of powerhouse female executives who would reshape the face of British television.

	“I didn’t think that I was leading a revolution. I just thought that I was going to make drama that I wanted to watch,” she said. “And if it’s drama that I want to watch, the drama should be inclusive of all. And in particular, I wanted to watch drama that had women in it.”

	The wide-ranging conversation touched on some of the iconic series that Tranter helped shepherd to the screen, from the HBO crime drama “The Night Of” (“It took two Obama presidencies to see it through”) to the multi-Emmy-winning “Succession” (“It was the best writers’ room I have ever experienced”) to “His Dark Materials,” the HBO fantasy adventure series that aired from 2019-2022 and “had a heartbeat to it that was speaking to where the world was going.”
	

	“It was the very, very early days of what we see so much of these days, where people are just thinking, ‘You know what? I don’t want that system. I don’t want to live in a way where the climate’s going to be destroyed. I don’t want to live in a way where my human rights are not given to me. I want to live in a different way,’” Tranter said.

	Asked about her decision to revive “Doctor Who” at the BBC in 2003, Tranter briefly gushed that she “loved the show” but otherwise steered clear of talk about the beloved series, whose future remains up in the air following the departure last year of Disney+ as a co-financier. Earlier this year, Tranter told Variety that Bad Wolf was commissioned to make 26 episodes of the series, insisting, “There was never any talk of more than that.” Last month, the BBC launched a competitive tender inviting pitches from producers to reboot the series. (Contacted by Variety following her appearance in Rome, Tranter’s team said she would not be answering any questions related to “Doctor Who.”)

	On stage at MIA, Tranter trumpeted the period drama “The Other Bennet Sister,” which is produced by Bad Wolf in association with the BBC and BritBox, as the latest example of her company reaching audiences by going against conventional wisdom.

	“If someone says to you, ‘You can’t make period drama. No one’s buying it. You can’t make fantasy. No one’s buying it. You can’t make a drama set in finance. No one will buy it.’ Make it. Just find a way and make it,” she said.

	Based on Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name, the series follows “Pride and Prejudice” protagonist Lizzie Bennet’s less charismatic sister Mary as she tries to step out of her family’s shadow and find her own place in the world. 

	Describing her as an “outsider” who’s “just slightly outside the norm,” Tranter heralded Mary — who’s played by “Call the Midwife’s” Ella Bruccoleri — as an example of an unconventional character “that people will respond to.” More importantly for the producer, she’s a woman who society “doesn’t really think should be an acceptable face of a woman.” 

	“Mary doesn’t look like people want a woman to look like. She doesn’t sound like people want a woman to sound like. She doesn’t behave like a society wants a woman to behave like. And yet Mary Bennet is her own woman,” Tranter said.
	

	“Stories about people being accepted for who they choose to be are the kind of stories that I will keep making until someone carries me out in a wooden box. And I would really urge you to keep making those kinds of stories,” she added. “We have to group together. We have to tell stories that will change the lack of empathy in our world. And if I leave you with anything from my ramblings about my career, it is to look into yourselves and go and tell your own stories that will make our world a more empathetic place.”

	The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market runs Oct. 19 – 23.

schema.headline: ‘Industry,’ ‘Doctor Who’ Producer Jane Tranter on Resisting Trends, Centering Women and Telling Stories About ‘People Being Accepted for Who They Choose to Be’

title: ‘Father’s House,’ Starring David Dencik and Trine-Dyrholm, Picked Up by DR Sales Ahead of Tallinn Competition
description: Copenhagen-based DR Sales, the international distributor of Oscar-winning doc “Mr Nobody Against Putin” and Sundance winner “A New Kind of Wilderne
body:
Copenhagen-based DR Sales, the international distributor of Oscar-winning doc “Mr Nobody Against Putin” and Sundance winner “A New Kind of Wilderness,” has boarded Denmark’s “Father’s House,” starring David Dencik (“No Time to Die,” “The Chestnut Man”) and Trine Dyrholm (“The Danish Woman,” “Queen of Hearts”).

	Selected for the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival international documentary competition and IDFA’s Signed section, “Father’s House” sees Dencik and Dyrholm acting in the reenactment scenes of a film which homes in on manipulation in a religious sect.
	

	“Father’s House” is co-directed by multi-awarded doc specialists Andreas Koefoed (“The Lost Leonardo,” “Music for Black Pigeons”), Eva Mulvad (“Enemies of Happiness,” “The Good Life”) and editor Adam Nielsen (“The Investigation,” “The Letter Room”).

	“We have been very excited about this project for some time. Once we saw the first cut, we were all blown away by how powerful and original the film is,” said DR Sales Executive Producer Kim Christiansen.

	A distinctive mix of fiction, documentary and making off, “Father’s House” (“Faderhuset”) looks at manipulation, abuse and often violence inside the radical Danish Christian sect Faderhuset, as three former members expose the inner workings of the now defunct sect where exorcism and speaking in tongues and militant Christianity were, reportedly, part of everyday life.

	Defining moments in the lives of the three characters within that closed sect are brought back to life via reenactments from established actors, under the guidance of the real former members.
	

	In a meta exercise. Dyrholm plays the charismatic leader Ruth Evensen (now Ruth Kristiansen) who led Fathers House since the 1990s until its official closure as a religious congregation in 2013. Dencik is the former member Jerry and Laura Kronborg Kjær (“A Fortunate Man,” “When the Sun Shines”) Camilla who stayed seven years within Father’s House before breaking away and setting up the NGO-InsideOut to help people leave such sectarian communities.

	Why Bring in Trine Dyrholm and David Dencik?Mulvad told Variety that the starting point to the film was a book written by former member Camilla Louise Johnson which sparked her interest in “cults, group dynamics and why people in a free world long to belong,” to the extent of surrendering their own lives.

	Depicted by Mulvad as “an important gatekeeper” throughout the filmmaking process, Camilla then introduced the directors to other former members of the sect who “shared their experience in a generous way” and contributed to the script.

	To avoid getting into “the long and lonely process of being a documentary director,” Mulvad rallied to her idea Koefoed, once the film’s hybrid concept was in place.

	“I found it very original and playful, and it gave me the opportunity to work in a new way,” said the helmer of the Tribeca-selected Sony Classics release “The Lost Leonardo.”

	Nielsen who had edited Mulvad’s Karlovy Vary winning doc “The Good Life” and Koefoed’s acclaimed “The Arms Drop,” joined, enjoying his first directing gig. “I was basically the rug from “The Big Lebowski” – the one tying the room together,” he quipped, before admitting: “It definitely gave me a taste for [directing].

	Quizzed about their choice to mix fiction and documentary, the co-helmers said, “What interested us most were the bizarre, insider stories from Father’s House. However, since no footage of those moments existed, we knew we didn’t want to rely on a traditional, interview-driven documentary. At the same time, we wanted to avoid a standard fiction film that forces real human experiences into a rigid plot. We wanted the best of both worlds.”

	As an editor, Nielsen took inspiration from his work on Kaspar Astrup’s documentary “The Invention of Dr. Nakamats” in which the eccentric Japanese inventor wanted to fictionalise a moment from his childhood, staging a scene with actors, while directing it himself on camera.“It was incredibly funny and surreal, and that meta-layered approach stayed with Adam,” said the co-helmers who were also inspired by a similar hybrid form in Kaouther Ben Haria’s “Four Daughters.”
	

	“We realised this approach could unlock our own narrative, so we decided to test it,” they said, outlining their technique. “We ran a pilot with actors Trine Dyrholm and Laura Kronborg Kjær interacting with the real ex- member Camilla Johnson. The dynamic between Camilla and the actors was electric, but the test also revealed something deeper: it became a profound way to expose how we manipulate reality when making films, whether fiction or documentary. By pulling back the curtain on our own process, the hybrid style allowed us to break free from a linear timeline and instead build the film around a purely emotional and psychological structure,” said the directing trio.

	The collaborative script was written in different steps, with the co-helmers adapting their fiction material to the real scenes depicted in detail by the former sect members, while the actors had to learn a new [religious] language, “where God, devil, praise, angels and so on take a dominant space.”

	‘Rich and Crazy’ Material

	“The material we got was rich and crazy,” said the filmmakers who decided “to look for dilemmas in the scenes, moments where the ex-members had to give up themselves to gain the trust of the leader or the group, moments of friction and existential doubt.”

	Asked about their personal take on Father’s House, Mulvad, Koefoed and Nielsen said, “Honestly, Father’s House isn’t fundamentally worse than many other religious sects or cults throughout history. What truly terrified us wasn’t just the group itself, but rather the lengths to which we as humans will go in our desperate search for love, acceptance and a sense of belonging.”

	They went on: “It’s comforting to look at the screen and think, ‘That would never happen to me.’ But the reality is that most of us have found ourselves in situations- – whether in relationships, jobs, or social circles – where boundaries were crossed, and we went far beyond our own sense of right and wrong.”

	Ultimately, the directing trio hope their film “will start a conversation about manipulative behaviour” and “lead the audience to start listening more to their gut feeling. It’s there for a reason,” they said. “At the end of the day, you can mess with people’s heads, you can gaslight them, but you can’t mess with their intuition. That’s what we want [the audience] to take away-trusting that inner voice.”
	

	Shopped as a 90-minute film or two-part series, “Father’s House” was produced by Pernille Rose Grønkjær and Malthe Koch for Danish Documentary and Nordic public broadcasters DR, NRK and SVT. The Danish release via Camera Film is slated for Nov. 19.

title: Leica and Formula 1 Team Up on $9,950 Camera Inspired by the Racetrack (Featuring Exclusive F1 Photo Setting)
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Formula 1
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Formula 1‘s luxury ambitions are extending to the camera business.

	Leica is the latest high-end brand to get in on the sport’s growing cultural cachet, teaming up with Formula 1 on a new licensing deal that will see the German camera maker release a $9,950 special-edition camera inspired by the racetrack.


						
			
	

	
					

	The Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition, available beginning Oct. 20, arrives as the racing league continues to build a business beyond the paddock, capitalizing on a surge in mainstream interest that has made Formula 1 an attractive partner for luxury brands. 


	The camera itself takes its design cues from the cockpit, with carbon-fiber detailing on its wireless charging handgrip, thumb rest and shutter button. Its black Microvelour covering is modeled after the textured surface of Formula 1 steering wheels, while red accents on the controls mimic the color-coded buttons used by drivers during races.

	There’s also an F1 logo stamped on the top plate and lens cap, a co-branded carrying strap and custom packaging with a red interior. The carbon-fiber components, which are manufactured and tested in Germany, mark a departure from materials traditionally used in Leica cameras.




	

	





	

	




	Leica has also developed an exclusive “Formula 1” photography setting that boosts contrast and color saturation to better capture the atmosphere of the racetrack. The effect can be previewed directly in the camera’s viewfinder and applied while shooting through the Leica FOTOS app, rather than added in post-production.

	Otherwise, the limited-edition model shares its technical foundation with the existing Leica Q3 43, including a fixed 43mm APO-Summicron f/2 lens, a full-frame sensor capable of shooting at 60, 36 or 18 megapixels, hybrid autofocus and video capabilities.

	Leica will introduce the camera at its Los Angeles store and gallery on Oct. 20, with Formula 1 presenter Ariana Bravo and former world champion Jenson Button on hand for the unveiling. The event will also include an exhibition of 26 racing photographs by Italian motorsport photographer Callo Albanese.


	The Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition will be available beginning Oct. 20 at Leica stores, the company’s online shop and specialist retailers for $9,950. It is compatible with existing Leica Q3 and Q3 43 accessories.

schema.headline: Leica and Formula 1 Team Up on $9,950 Camera Inspired by the Racetrack (Featuring Exclusive F1 Photo Setting)

title: ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work
description: Asia Kate Dillon, who starred in shows like “Orange Is the New Black” and “Billions,” took to social media on Tuesday to share that they are lookin
body:
Asia Kate Dillon, who starred in shows like “Orange Is the New Black” and “Billions,” took to social media on Tuesday to share that they are looking for service work after their acting work “has all but diminished” after eleven years in the industry.

	Dillon began their statement by going through previous service jobs they’ve held, from dishwasher to floor manager to food runner. “When I was fifteen, I got my first job in food service,” they wrote, and stayed in the industry until they were able to support themselves full-time as an actor.
	

	“I continued working in food and general customer service, alongside any acting gigs I could rustle up, until the fall of 2015 when I was finally able to make the transition to a full time income stemming from just my acting work. I have worked exclusively in theater, film and TV for the last eleven years,” Dillon continued. “Now, like for many, many performer colleagues of mine — particularly those of us who are trans/nonbinary/gender nonconforming — acting work has all but diminished, and I’m in need of service work once more.”


	Dillon first appeared in single episodes of shows like “Younger,” “Opus for All” and “Master of None” before booking “Orange Is the New Black,” which they went on to star in for 19 episodes as Brandy Epps. In 2017, they landed the role of Taylor Mason on “Billions,” which they played across six seasons and 71 episodes. Dillon also had roles in “John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum,” “The Outside Story” and “Gen: Lock,” and starred in the film “Outerlands” in 2025.
	

	In late 2026, Dillon publicly came out as non-binary. They were the first gender nonbinary performer to play a nonbinary character on a major TV show. In 2020, the actor called for the SAG Awards (now known as the Actor Awards) to abolish gender-specific categories, writing that “separating people based on their assigned sex, and/or their gender identity, is not only irrelevant when it comes to how an acting performance should be judged, it is also a form of discrimination.”

	Read Dillon’s full statement here.

	Hello!

	In the year 2000, when I was fifteen, I got my first job in food service. It was a weekend gig at the (locally) famous, always bustling Ithaca Bakery. I worked mornings; first up was sorting the freshly baked piping hot bagels in their respective bins, and then I would move into rotating and stocking the drink fridges. Throughout my shift my duties included maintaining the coffee station in the center of the retail floor – lids, sugars, straws, stirrers, sleeves, I kept everything very tidy – cleaning and restocking the restroom, mopping up inevitable customer spills, ferrying dirty and then clean dish bins to and from the dining areas, and greeting customers. I loved it.

	Ranging from dishwasher to food runner to floor manager, I continued working in food and general customer service, alongside any acting gigs I could rustle up, until the fall of 2015 when I was finally able to make the transition to a full time income stemming from just my acting work. I have worked exclusively in theater, film and TV for the last eleven years.

	Now, like for many, many performer colleagues of mine – particularly those of us who are trans/nonbinary/gender nonconforming – acting work has all but diminished, and I’m in need of service work once more.

	I love customer service. I love creating welcoming environments for people to relax in and connect with each other. I love food and drink. I am passionate and curious, and a great teammate. I imagine the hurdle to reentry will be learning the new POS systems, but I’m a quick study. I’m available for part time, night and weekend work.

	Thanks in advance for your consideration.

	All best,

	Asia Kate Dillon

	(they/them)

schema.headline: ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work

title: ‘Pirates of the Caribbean’ Secret Cinema Immersive Stage Show Casts George Maguire as Jack Sparrow, Extends London Run
description: Olivier winner George Maguire will play Captain Jack Sparrow in “Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: The Immersive Adventure,” the London stage prod
body:
Olivier winner George Maguire will play Captain Jack Sparrow in “Disney’s Pirates of the Caribbean: The Immersive Adventure,” the London stage production from Secret Cinema and TodayTix. 

	Phil Daniels, known for “Quadrophenia,” “EastEnders” and Blur’s “Parklife,” will play Captain Barbossa. Lily Blunsom is Elizabeth Swann, Harrison Wilde is Will Turner and Gleanne Purcell-Brown is Anamaria. The rest of the cast will be named later. Matt Costain, also an Olivier winner, directs. 
	

	Previews begin Feb. 16, and the show opens on March 10 at Secret Cinema’s new riverside venue on the Greenwich Peninsula. The production is the first at the site, which the company plans to keep as its home. Strong demand has led the producers to add six weeks to the run.


	No earlier stage version of the franchise has been fully immersive, and the show marks a change of approach for Secret Cinema. Live storytelling leads the show. Instead of screening the whole of “Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl,” the production uses selected clips from the film alongside large set pieces. Over two hours, audiences can roam the sets, meet characters and take part in the story, with stunts and a live band.

	The creative team includes two-time Emmy winner Jason Sherwood as production designer. His credits include live broadcasts of the Oscars and “Rent Live.” Kait Kerrigan, who wrote the book for Broadway’s “The Great Gatsby,” is the theatrical adaptor. Olivier winner Alan Williams handles music supervision, arrangements and orchestrations. Stuart Burt is casting director, Susan Kulkarni designs costumes, Helen Keane of Campbell Young Associates designs wigs, hair and makeup, and Alex Payne is fight director.
	

	“We’ve taken everything Secret Cinema does best and pushed it further than ever before, creating a new kind of theatrical experience where the story doesn’t just happen in front of you – it happens all around you,” said Merritt Baer, Secret Cinema’s artistic director and producer and president and co-founder of TodayTix Group. “This is exactly the kind of show we’ve been building towards and opening it in our new home at Greenwich Peninsula makes it even more exciting.”

	Maguire won his Olivier for playing Dave Davies in the musical “Sunny Afternoon.” His screen credits include “EastEnders,” “Prime Suspect” and “Borgia.” Daniels’ other film work includes “Chicken Run” and “Scum,” and he appears with Olivia Colman in “Wicker,” due out in 2026.

	The production is licensed through Disney Theatrical Group. Angelo Desimini, the group’s senior VP of licensed partnerships and brand management, said Disney was excited by the chance to bring the franchise’s spirit to life through theatrical talent and immersive storytelling. “Secret Cinema has assembled a remarkable team to create an experience that is both artistically ambitious and wonderfully entertaining,” Desimini said. “It’s a chance for audiences to experience the world of Tortuga in an entirely new way.”

	TodayTix bought Secret Cinema in 2022. Baer took charge of the company in 2024, and since then it has staged “Grease: The Immersive Movie Musical,” its most popular production in 19 years. Its more than 70 shows also include “Stranger Things,” “Guardians of the Galaxy: The Live Experience” and “Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back.”

schema.headline: ‘Pirates of the Caribbean’ Secret Cinema Immersive Stage Show Casts George Maguire as Jack Sparrow, Extends London Run

title: Park Min-young, Yook Sung-jae, Go Soo Lead Prime Video Korean Office Romance ‘Nine to Six’
description: Park Min-young, the star of “Marry My Husband,” will lead “Nine to Six,” a Korean office romance. Yook Sung-jae of K-pop group BtoB and Go Soo co-s
body:
Park Min-young, the star of “Marry My Husband,” will lead “Nine to Six,” a Korean office romance. Yook Sung-jae of K-pop group BtoB and Go Soo co-star in the 12-episode series.

	Park plays Kang Yi-ji, a senior manager on the legal team at a company called Chronic Motors. Logical and driven, Yi-ji has carved out her place in a workplace dominated by men and regards love and marriage as little more than a passing chemical impulse. She once wanted to study astronomy but went into law because her mother pushed her toward it.
	

	Two men upend her orderly routine.


	Yook plays Han Sun-woo, a legal intern who would rather be designing jewelry and who trusts his instincts over logic. When Yi-ji is put in danger, he shields her without a second thought, and she may start to view him differently.

	Go plays Park Hyun-tae, an executive director in Chronic Motors’ Seoul office who has come back from the company’s European headquarters after climbing the corporate ladder at a young age. Hyun-tae has long been convinced that romance only complicates life. Yi-ji, whose competence wins his respect, puts that view to the test.

	The series sets the younger colleague’s openness against the executive’s grasp of her ambitions, leaving Yi-ji to work out whether she can let someone in without sacrificing the career she has spent years building.

	Choi Ji-oh wrote the series. Lee Hyung-min, whose credits include “Strong Girl Bong-soon,” “Miss Night and Day” and “I’m Sorry, I Love You,” directs alongside Oh Song-hee (“The Escape of the Seven”).
	

	The series debuts on Prime Video on Nov. 25 across 240-plus countries and territories.

	Park’s other credits include “Siren’s Kiss” and “Confidence Queen.” Yook has appeared in “The Haunted Palace,” “The Golden Spoon” and “Guardian: The Lonely and Great God,” while Go’s work includes “Missing: The Other Side,” “Colony” and “Parole Examiner Lee.”

	“Nine to Six” joins a Prime Video lineup that already carries “Love in Disguise,” “A Love Other Than Yours,” “See You at Work Tomorrow!,” “Spring Fever,” “Surely Tomorrow,” “Head Over Heels” and “Good Boy.”

schema.headline: Park Min-young, Yook Sung-jae, Go Soo Lead Prime Video Korean Office Romance ‘Nine to Six’

title: Thai Pop Star Jeff Satur Signs With Universal Music Southeast Asia, Sets 2027 Album and World Tour
description: Thai singer-songwriter and actor Jeff Satur, whose music has passed 2 billion streams, has signed with Universal Music Southeast Asia (UM SEA), the
body:
Thai singer-songwriter and actor Jeff Satur, whose music has passed 2 billion streams, has signed with Universal Music Southeast Asia (UM SEA), the regional division of Universal Music Group, as he pushes to take T-pop to a global audience.

	The first major release under the new deal will be Satur’s second studio album, slated for the second quarter of 2027. A debut solo stadium show in Bangkok will follow, and a world tour will run from late 2027 into 2028.
	

	UM SEA will back Satur across a wide range of areas. That covers shaping his music and creative direction, marketing and publicity, building his audience, touring, business opportunities and collaborations with leading producers and artists. Satur was previously signed to Wayfer Records, part of Warner Music Thailand.


	“At this point in my career, it was important for me to find a partner that truly understands my vision, one that can help me bring my ideas to life without losing what makes them mine,” Satur said. “I’m excited for Saturn to meet the Universe and begin the next chapter of creating without borders, because at its heart, music has always been my universal language.”

	Satur, who also produces, is known for tracks including “Fade,” “Dum Dum,” “Hide,” “Ghost” and “Black Tie,” and has built a fan following across Asia, the U.S. and Latin America. His 2025 Red Giant Tour played Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Brazil, Chile, Mexico and Peru. At home, it included two sold-out shows at Bangkok’s Impact Arena, Thailand’s largest indoor arena.
	

	This year, Satur was the first Thai artist to appear at Global Spin Live, a conversation-and-performance event at L.A.’s Grammy Museum, and to play live on “Good Day New York,” the TV program on New York’s WNYW Fox 5.

	Adam Granite, CEO of Universal Music Group for Africa, the Middle East and Asia, said: “Jeff Satur is an exceptional artist whose creativity and international appeal reflect the enormous potential of Thai music today. This partnership reinforces our commitment to investing in high-potential Thai artists and helping them reach audiences around the world. We are delighted to welcome him to the UMG family and look forward to working with him to achieve even greater success on the world stage.”

	Calvin Wong, CEO of Universal Music Southeast Asia and Korea and senior VP for Asia, called Satur one of Thailand’s most exciting and distinctive artists, with an impressive career and a passionate international fanbase. “We see tremendous potential to take his journey even further with the strength of UMG’s global network behind him,” Wong said. “We’re excited to work with him to expand his reach across Asia and around the world, and help him on his journey to becoming a global superstar.”

schema.headline: Thai Pop Star Jeff Satur Signs With Universal Music Southeast Asia, Sets 2027 Album and World Tour

title: ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’
description: “Young Sheldon” actor Iain Armitage might’ve become a star thanks to the hit CBS sitcom, but when it came time to call it quits on the seven-season
body:
“Young Sheldon” actor Iain Armitage might’ve become a star thanks to the hit CBS sitcom, but when it came time to call it quits on the seven-season series in 2024, he admits he was the cast member “the most happy about the show ending.”

	In an interview featured in Jessica Radloff’s oral history, “Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy” (via US Weekly), Armitage, who played the titular character, said he wasn’t “going home and crying all day” like some of his co-workers at the news of the series ending. He also added that it was “heavy and annoying and weird” to be in a state of mourning around “Young Sheldon,” and he refused to “stay in that heaviness forever.”
	

	“Plus, I wanted to be in Virginia. I wanted to be traveling, and I’m happy to do whatever movie comes up. And my mom has always imbued me with a very healthy sense of ephemerality, and the fact that nothing good can last and everything changes, and that’s a good thing,” he said. “I would hate to be on a show playing 23-year-old Sheldon. That would suck. I wouldn’t want to do that.”


	Armitage was just eight years old when the series began, and now, two years since it ended, he said he it’s “nostalgic sad” to look back. “I miss working at Warner Bros., I miss the crew and the people I love. I love the act of acting. I love doing it. It’s fun. But not really specific moments. More the overall thing.”

	“And Iain was ready, too … to move on to something else, artistically, and maybe personally … with things that boiled up a little bit toward the end of the season,” said Lance Barber, who played George Sr., Sheldon’s dad, in the book. “I think a lot of people felt there were certain elements of the show that they were ready to move on from.”
	

	In a previously released excerpt of Radloff’s novel, Armitage said that while it was a “complete privilege” to be on the show, it was a “big undertaking for an 8-year-old.” “I always did the best that I could, and sometimes kids are not perfect,” he continued. “I was grateful to the people who understood that and gave me grace.”

	“Young Sheldon” was so successful that the Sheldon Cooper-focused “Big Bang Theory” prequel inspired its own spinoff, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” which premiered in 2024.

schema.headline: ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Iain Armitage Says He Was the ‘Most Happy’ About the Show Ending: I Wasn’t ‘Going Home and Crying All Day’

title: Julia Stiles ‘Bawled’ Before Heath Ledger Tribute, Breaks Down ‘10 Things I Hate About You’ Cast Reunion on ‘Dancing With the Stars’
description:
Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.”

	During Dedication Night, she performed
body:
Julia Stiles paid tribute to the late Heath Ledger on Tuesday night’s episode of “Dancing With the Stars.”

	During Dedication Night, she performed a contemporary routine with her partner Ezra Sosa to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You”; in the 1999 film “10 Things I Hate About You,” Ledger’s character, Patrick, sang the Frankie Valli number to Stiles’ Kat Stratford from the bleachers while she was at soccer practice.




	

									©Touchstone Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	“I said, if we had to have someone with us on stage representing Heath’s legacy or the film, I said it had to be the whole cast. I begged them, each and every one of them, and they all rallied. They really did,” Stiles told Variety after the routine. She said that it was “really trippy” to see herself in the blue dress, similar to what she wore in the film, and her hair done in a similar style. “At 17 years old, I never would have thought that I’d be here at 45, celebrating my body, dancing on the show that I absolutely love and that fans are still interested in this movie and still moved and touched by this movie.”
	

	Earlier in the week, Stiles opened up to Variety about the emotional rehearsals.

	“I know that Dedication Night is emotional, but I thought I was distanced from it enough. Like, oh, it was so many years ago. Something about seeing clips from that movie and images and hearing my voice and hearing his voice is bringing back so many memories. It’s a lot,” she said, noting that she started crying while practicing. “One of the things that we really hope to do as performers is to make people feel something and have people care about the work that you do, and his memory lives on because it was such an incredible performance.”
	

	Ledger died in January 2008 at the age of 28.

schema.headline: Julia Stiles ‘Bawled’ Before Heath Ledger Tribute, Breaks Down ‘10 Things I Hate About You’ Cast Reunion on ‘Dancing With the Stars’

title: Netflix Chiefs Concede That Slowdown in U.S. Viewing Sparked the Content Leadership Shakeup: ‘We’re Focusing on Execution,’ Ted Sarandos Says
description: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters nodded to slowdown in U.S. viewing and ad sales that spurred the radical shake-up of the streamer’s co
body:
Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters nodded to slowdown in U.S. viewing and ad sales that spurred the radical shake-up of the streamer’s content leadership during Tuesday’s conversation with Wall Street analysts after its third-quarter earnings release.

	Sarandos and Peters had to address the situation that led to the dramatic decision to oust chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin. Former Fox and Disney executive Peter Rice was appointed Oct. 15 as Bajaria’s successor, starting next week.
	

	Peters sought to assure analysts that while Netflix is going through a soft period in the U.S., its underlying fundamentals are strong. As ever, when the going gets tough in pay TV, executives point to positive signs when it comes to churn — or the lack thereof. Peters emphasized that the churn rate of subscribers moving on and off the platform was better than expected in the U.S. and elsewhere for the quarter, especially after the streamer initiated a price hike.


	Peters emphasized that “the quality, quantity and variety of viewing remains healthy and it drives our business model. And the best evidence that we’ve got that we’re delivering that value is churn. We’ve got healthy retention in every region,” he said. For the quarter ended Sept. 30, the level of churn improved on a global basis and in the U.S.

	“The ultimate determinant of are we delivering that value is the reaction to price changes. And those recent price changes that we did, including in the United States, have gone well. We’ve seen results that are consistent with past changes,” Peters said. 
	

	Most of the regions outside the U.S. delivered strong viewing and engagement, he added. 

	“Our local titles from those regions are driving engagement and they’re driving business growth. And you can see how our business model works here. We specifically highlighted India, which had a strong slate with a couple titles really, really performing. And as a result, view hours in Q3 in India grew 24% on an absolute basis,” Peters said. “They were also up on a per-member basis, all of which drives membership.”

	As the dust settles on the management shake-up, Sarandos told analysts that they are laser-focused on nurturing shows to stand out as hits.

	“We had some really solid doubles and triples this year, but the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they’ll travel around the world. We’re focusing on that execution,” Sarandos said. “India is a great example, but that success is also happening in Korea and Japan. And when you look to [Europe, the Middle East and Africa], when we look to the Nordics, which is a very mature market for us, that content slate is killing it there. And it’s proof that when we have the right focus, make the right choices and deliver creatively, we can drive outsize impact on the business around the world.”

	Rice, Sarandos added, “brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s that exact skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter.”

	Spencer Neumann, Netflix’s chief financial officer, chimed in with his observation that while Netflix does need big, noisy hits, it is not overly dependent on any one genre or format of content.

	“Even with modest view-hour growth that we’re delivering, we’re delivering that increasing value to our members across quality, quantity and variety viewing with a steady drumbeat of big hits in most regions,” Neumann said. “That’s really the great thing about our model — the stability of our growth engine. We’re not overly dependent on any kind of one title, nor outsized performance by any one region to deliver healthy growth.”

	(Pictured: Netflix co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos)

schema.headline: Netflix Chiefs Concede That Slowdown in U.S. Viewing Sparked the Content Leadership Shakeup: ‘We’re Focusing on Execution,’ Ted Sarandos Says

title: Reality Star Kash's Mom Says Sister Wishes She Could Trade Places With Her After Fatal Shooting
description:

                          Wishes
body:
Kash's Mom
                          Says Daughter Who Shot Kash
                          Wishes She Could Trade Places With Reality Star
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 21, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Reality star Kash’s sister who is charged with her death is devastated over her passing ... and their mom tells TMZ she’s so distraught over the fatal shooting, she’s repeatedly wished she could trade places with her late sister.
      
    
            Kash’s mom, Cynthia, tells TMZ ... she’s spoken with and visited her daughter, Vernika Dunbar, in jail since the shooting, and says Vernika has been crying and struggling to believe what happened.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Cynthia says Vernika repeatedly expresses how much she loves Kash and wishes she could switch places with her. Their mom says she’s reminded Vernika she still has children who need her and an entire family that loves her.
      

            As we reported ... Kash was fatally shot in Oakland on October 11 during an altercation with another woman. Police say Vernika grabbed a gun from someone in their group and attempted to pistol-whip the woman during the fight ... but the weapon discharged, striking Kash in the head.
      
    
            Kash was rushed to a hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Vernika was arrested and charged with involuntary manslaughter, assault with a firearm, and carrying a loaded firearm in public, all felonies. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Cynthia describes her family as extremely close-knit and insists there was never any drama or bad blood between the sisters. She says they loved spending time together, making the circumstances of Kash’s death especially difficult for everyone to process.
      
    
            In fact, Cynthia says the family spent the day at her granddaughter’s flag football game before the shooting. Later that night, Kash and Vernika were singing songs together and enjoying themselves at a motorcycle club with their mom.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Cynthia says nobody went out expecting violence or imagined the night would end in tragedy. She’s also seen video circulating online and the social media coverage surrounding her daughter’s death.
      
    
            Despite the criminal case against Vernika, Cynthia maintains the shooting was an accident and insists her daughter never intended to harm her sister. For now, she says the family is mourning Kash while continuing to support Vernika.

title: Aaron Carter's Estate Allegedly Owes 6-Figure Tax Debt
description:

                          IRS Says His Estate Owes $461K
body:
Aaron Carter
                          IRS Says His Estate Owes $461K
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 21, 2026
                            12:30 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Aaron Carter's estate is on the taxman's radar ... the IRS says they're owed nearly $500K in taxes, interest, and penalties.
      
    
            According to new documents filed by the IRS and obtained by TMZ, Aaron had several unpaid tax balances from 2014, 2018, 2019, 2020, and 2021.
      
    
            The 2014 balance is a mere $326.60 ... but the amounts owed get progressively larger -- including $172,538.70 owed between the balance, interest, and penalties for 2021.
      
    
            All told, Uncle Sam says it's owed $461,253.54 ... and it's filed the doc with the court in an effort to collect.
      
    
            We broke the story ... Aaron passed away back in November 2022 -- and there's been a fight over his estate ever since.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Aaron's mother, Jane Schneck, actually fought to keep the estate operating earlier this year ... but it was closed after a judge ruled it was insolvent. His ex, Melanie Martin, received all non-cash assets.
      
    
            Jane believed the trustee in charge had undervalued the value of Aaron's royalties. She also alleged Melanie had made "illegal withdrawals" from Aaron’s accounts totaling $24,530.
      
    
            Given the context, it's unclear how the IRS expects the estate to pay the tax bill. We've reached out to Carter's estate for more information.
